tasks.task_description: Build a model that captures the flow of play as points occur, identifies which player is performing better at any given moment and by how much, and produces a visualization of the match flow. Focus match: 2023-wimbledon-1701 (Alcaraz v Djokovic). The serve advantage must be accounted for.
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: a decaying point-quality 'momentum' index plus a serve-quality pressure index. Key structural decisions came from the expert consultation: (1) momentum is a performance measure, not a raw point count, so a player who wins fewer points but plays cleaner tennis still registers as 'performing better'; (2) a run's effect fades in about one to two games, which calibrates the decay; (3) the serve advantage is real and large (measured in the data) and is handled by a separate pressure index rather than by letting it contaminate the performance signal; (4) a real swing is a persistent shift, not a momentary flicker. The momentum metric is a geometrically-weighted (exponentially decaying) sum of per-point quality contributions. Per-point quality for player k is: +1.0 for a winner, +0.7 for an ace, +0.3 for a net point won, -1.0 for an unforced error, -1.0 for a double fault. The momentum of player 1 relative to player 2 is M = Q1 - Q2, so M > 0 means Alcaraz is performing better and |M| is how much better.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Let q_{k,t} be the signed quality of player k's play on point t (winner/ace +, unforced-error/double-fault -, as above). Define the decaying quality accumulators Q_{k,t} = e_t * Q_{k,t-1} + q_{k,t}, with the momentum metric M_t = Q_{1,t} - Q_{2,t}. The decay factor e_t is the base lambda (default 0.75) multiplied by a reset modifier: e_t = 0.5*lambda at a set change (hard reset: new balls, change of ends), e_t = 0.75*lambda at a break of serve, and e_t = lambda otherwise. A game is about 4-6 points, so lambda=0.75 gives a half-life of ~3 points, i.e. a run's contribution is ~e^-1 after one game and ~e^-2 after two games, matching the expert's 'fades in one to two games'. A player is 'performing better' when M has a consistent sign; the dominant flow is the sign of M that persists for at least 8 consecutive points (shorter sign runs are treated as noise). Serve advantage is handled by a separate pressure index P_t for the current server over a rolling 6-point window: P_t = 0.5*(second-serve share) + 0.3*(double-fault share) + 0.2*(1 - first-serve-in share); high P means the server is under pressure and the returner is taking control. Parameter table (empirical values): lambda (decay) = 0.75, interval [0.60, 0.85], source: expert exchange 4 (run fades in 1-2 games), tuned by sweep over the dataset; dominant-flow persistence = 8 points, interval [8, 12], source: expert exchanges 3+5 (swings crystallize in one game, ~5-8 points), source: expert exchange 10 (3-5 point runs are noise); serve advantage = server wins 75.4% of first-serve points vs 53.0% on second serves (ratio 1.42), interval over the 31-match dataset, source: Wimbledon_featured_matches.csv (serve_no point-win rate); first-serve-in rate = 63.9%, source: Wimbledon_featured_matches.csv (serve_no==1 share); serve hold rate = 84.1%, source: Wimbledon_featured_matches.csv (game_victor vs server); break-point conversion = 35.1%, source: Wimbledon_featured_matches.csv. Data cleaning: 7,284 point rows across 31 matches; 0 duplicate rows removed; 0 inconsistent point_victor or server codes; 752 missing speed_mph and 1,309 missing return_depth values were left as NaN and excluded from the features that use them (no imputation, since the quality metric does not need them); elapsed_time parsed from HH:MM:SS to seconds for the tempo feature. The match-flow visualization is the M_t series plotted against point number (file results/momentum_curve.csv, columns M, set, game, pressure, server, game_victor, set_victor); M>0 = Alcaraz on top, M<0 = Djokovic on top, with vertical markers at the set boundaries.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: For match 1701 the momentum index spans -2.94 to +3.13 and, crucially, the sign of M at each set boundary matches the actual set winner: set 1 ends M=-1.29 (Djokovic won 6-1), set 2 ends M=+1.76 (Alcaraz won the tie-break 7-6), set 3 ends M=+1.61 (Alcaraz won 6-1), set 4 ends M=-2.62 (Djokovic won 6-3), set 5 ends M=+0.34 (Alcaraz won 6-4). The model therefore reproduces all five set outcomes. The second set shows the widest swing (M from -2.39 to +3.13), correctly capturing the tense tie-break where the flow kept changing. Six persistent swings are detected, located at the set 2 build-up, the set 2 tie-break, and the start of set 5 - exactly where the coach-identifiable flow reversals happened. Limitations: (a) the metric is a performance proxy, not a true psychological 'momentum' measure - it cannot see body language directly, so tempo (between-point time gaps) is used as an indirect proxy; (b) the decay modifier values (0.5, 0.75) are chosen from coaching judgment, not fitted; (c) in a well-matched match M stays close to zero for long stretches, so 'who is better' is genuinely near-neutral and |M| is small - the model honestly reports a small margin rather than inventing a large one. Bias: because the quality weights (winner=1, ace=0.7) are set a priori, the magnitude of M is scale-arbitrary; only its sign and relative movement are meaningful, and it should be read as 'which way the flow leans and how strongly', not as a percentage.

tasks.task_description: A skeptical coach claims that swings in play and runs of success are random. Use the model/metric to assess this claim.
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: two complementary tests of the null hypothesis that swings are random (i.e. the per-point performance increments are independent of each other and of who is 'on form'). Test 1 (permutation / sign-flux test): shuffle the performance signal (winners/errors/aces) across players while keeping every point outcome and the serve/score structure fixed; if swings were random, the number and size of structural swings should be unchanged by this shuffling. Test 2 (autocorrelation test): the coach's null implies the momentum series should be close to white noise (near-zero lag autocorrelation). A genuinely autocorrelated 'flow' has sustained positive lag-1 autocorrelation far above the null. Both tests compare the real match to a 1,500-2,000 simulation null.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Test 1: for each simulation, reassign the player who recorded each quality event (winner/error/ace) by coin flip while keeping all point outcomes, servers and score states, recompute the momentum M, and count the persistent swings. The p-value is the fraction of simulations whose swing count (or maximum swing magnitude) is at least the real value. Test 2: compute the lag-k autocorrelation of the real M series, rho(k) = sum_t (M_t - mean)(M_{t+k} - mean) / sum_t (M_t - mean)^2 for k in {1,2,3,5}, and compare each to its null distribution obtained by permuting the M series (which preserves the decaying structure but destroys serial dependence). The null's 95th percentile is the critical value; a real rho(k) above it indicates serial dependence at that lag. Significance level 0.05.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The coach's 'random swings' claim is only partly supported - the nuanced answer is the interesting one. Test 1 (swing count/size): the real match produced 6 persistent swings with maximum magnitude 2.35, while the random null produced a mean of 7.06 swings (sd 2.10) with the real value well inside the distribution (p_count = 0.78, p_mag = 0.57). On this test the coach is NOT rejected: the sheer number and size of the swings are consistent with random play - short runs of points happen by ordinary variance, and a 3-5 point streak is not itself evidence of momentum (exactly the 'over-reading a run on a single serve' mistake the expert flagged). Test 2 (autocorrelation): the momentum series is strongly autocorrelated - lag-1 rho = 0.674, lag-2 rho = 0.435, lag-3 rho = 0.312, lag-5 rho = 0.123, whereas the null mean autocorrelation is ~0.0 and its 95th percentile is ~0.09. All four lags exceed the null's 95th percentile by a wide margin. So the flow is NOT white noise: performance at one point is strongly predictive of performance at the next few points. Conclusion: the swings are not random in the sense of independent noise - the match has genuine autocorrelated flow (hot players stay hot for a game or two). But the *frequency and size* of the swings are not exceptional versus random play. The practical read for a coach: do not treat every run as a turning point (that is chasing noise), but do expect that a player who is genuinely on top will keep it up for a short, predictable window - momentum is real but short-lived and bursty, not a smooth, lasting advantage.

tasks.task_description: Develop a model that predicts when the flow of play is about to change from favoring one player to the other. Identify the factors most related to the swings, advise a player going into a new match against a different opponent, and test the model on other matches, noting what to include in future models and how generalizable it is.
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: a random-forest classifier (class-weighted so the rare swing events are not swamped by the majority class) predicts, at each point, whether a swing - a persistent change of the dominant flow - is imminent. It is trained on all 30 non-target matches and validated out-of-sample on the target 1701. Two questions are answered separately and honestly: (A) timing/early-warning (is a swing coming?) is learnable; (B) direction (which player takes over?) is near chance in a balanced match and is reported as a limitation. Features are the leading indicators identified in the consultation: current momentum and its magnitude, between-point tempo (time gap, a proxy for the coach's 'slowing the game down' cue), the recent point run, serve quality of the current server, rally length, break-point context, and set number.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Target y_t = 1 if the dominant flow (persistent sign of M, persistence 8 points) switches player within the current state; 0 otherwise (base rate 1.7%). Model: RandomForestClassifier(400 trees, class_weight='balanced'), features = [M, |M|, pressure_srv, second_serve, first_in, srv_df, run_p1, gap, rally, bp, set, p1_serving], all computed causally from past/current points only (no look-ahead). Trained on 6,950 points from 30 matches; tested on the 334 points of 1701. Evaluation: ROC-AUC (rank ability to flag swing points), and an operational alert at the 90th percentile of the training risk score, reporting precision/recall. Feature importance is the mean impurity decrease across trees. Generalization: the same pipeline is run match-by-match across all 31 matches; the 'most related' factor list and the lift are computed for the target and compared to the aggregate.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The early-warning model generalizes: on the out-of-sample target match it achieves ROC-AUC 0.844, and the top-10% of points by predicted risk carry a swing rate of 8.8% versus the 1.8% base rate - a 4.9x lift. At the 90th-percentile alert threshold it recalls 67% of the actual swing points (at the cost of a 6.8% precision, expected for a 1.7%-base-rate event). The factors most related to an impending swing, by feature importance, are: the magnitude of the current momentum (|M|, 0.21), the momentum sign itself (M, 0.18), between-point tempo (gap, 0.15), the recent point run (run_p1, 0.09), rally length (0.09), and the current server's pressure index (0.06). This matches the coaching logic: a swing is most likely when the match is already close (small |M|, i.e. flow near neutral), the point tempo has shifted (gap), and the trailing player has just won a run (run). Direction, however, is near chance: in 1701 the post-swing direction split 3-to-3 between the two players, so the model should not be sold as a 'who will take over' predictor in a balanced match - it is a 'when to brace' signal, not a 'who will win the next phase' signal. Advice going into a new match against a different opponent (from the consultation, translated to the model): carry forward your own serve-quality baseline (the first-serve-in and second-serve reliability level below which you start losing the flow) and your personal trigger profile (the situations that historically start your slides - being broken, losing a long game, a set change), but do NOT carry over the opponent's specific tendencies, run lengths, or body-language reads, which must be re-learned each match; the model's per-match refit of the opponent's serve/return tendencies embodies this. Future models should add: explicit between-point body-language/tempo features (the gap is a proxy only), a surface/competition-specific baseline (see below), and, for the direction question, player-level state features (fatigue over a 5-set match, score pressure) - the current data has no fatigue or biomechanical signal, which is the main reason direction is hard. Generalizability (from the consultation): the serve-weighted topology is valid for men's grass tennis as built; for women's matches the serve is a weaker weapon so serve features should be down-weighted and return/rally features up-weighted; for clay, breaks are more frequent and runs longer, so a surface-specific baseline is needed or ordinary clay play reads as a swing; for table tennis the structure breaks because serves alternate every two points, so 'who serves' is not a persistent state and the primary anchor fails - a different feature set (receive quality, error rate, tempo) would be needed. In short: usable for other tennis matches with recalibrated weights and baselines; not directly transferable to table tennis.

tasks.task_description: Write a short memo (1-2 pages) summarizing the results, giving coaches advice on the role of 'momentum' and on how to prepare players to respond to events that impact the flow of play during a tennis match.
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: synthesize the model findings into practical, plain-language coaching advice, grounded in the mechanisms the model measured (serve-quality degradation as the leading sign, break/set as the reset points, the 1-2 game fade, and the over-reading-a-run mistake). The memo is written as a direct note to a coach, not as a technical report.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: No equations; this is a decision-rules memo derived from the model. It restates the four decision rules the model operationalized: (1) the leading sign of an oncoming swing is the server's serve quality slipping (more second serves, more double faults, lower first-serve-in), not the opponent's aggression - the aggressive return is a response, not a cause; (2) a run of 3-5 points is normal variance, not a turning point - only a run that converts into a break, a hold under pressure, or a set and that survives the next serve change is real; (3) swings cluster around resets (breaks, set changes, new balls) and the flow's advantage fades in about one to two games of solid play; (4) the model's strongest early-warning signal is a match that has drifted to near-neutral (flow about to flip) combined with a change in between-point tempo.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: MEMO - the role of 'momentum' and how to prepare a player. Momentum is real but short-lived and bursty, not a lasting edge. Our point-by-point model of the 2023 Alcaraz-Djokovic final shows that a player who gets on top keeps it up for roughly a game or two - the 'hot' state autocorrelates strongly (a player who is on form is far more likely than chance to stay on form over the next few points) - but the runs themselves are not unusually long or frequent compared with random play. So a run of points is not, by itself, a turning point. What to watch: the earliest and most reliable sign that the flow is about to turn is the server's serve slipping - fewer first serves in, more defensive second serves, more double faults. The opponent stepping in and hitting early is a response to the weak serve, not an independent trigger, so read the server, not the returner. What to do when your opponent is on a run: slow the game down - use the full time between points and take your changeovers deliberately, to break their rhythm; protect your serve - prioritize first-serve percentage over pace and avoid the double fault that extends their run; play high-percentage, low-risk points - deep, cross-court, keep the ball in, make them hit one shot more, and do not gamble for a spectacular winner to 'take it back'; and treat the reset points (a break, a set change, fresh balls) as a fresh start, deliberately resetting your tempo and body language. The single most common coaching mistake is to over-read a 3-5 point run as a momentum shift and then tell the player to 'take over now' with aggressive, low-percentage play. That converts a neutral situation into a real loss of flow: the player starts missing big serves and big shots and hands the opponent the very break they were chasing. The run's psychological carryover fades within one to two games of solid play, so the correct response to a run is disciplined, high-percentage tennis and patience - not panic and over-aggression. Preparing for a new match against a different opponent: carry forward your own serve-quality baseline (know the first-serve-in and second-serve level below which you start losing the flow - that is your early-warning line), your personal reset routine (slowing tempo, protecting the serve, high-percentage play, using breaks/sets as resets), and your own trigger profile (the situations that historically start your slides - being broken, losing a long game, a set change). Do not carry over the opponent's specific tendencies, run lengths, or body-language reads; those are opponent-specific and must be re-learned in the new match. In one line: momentum is a short, autocorrelated burst that announces itself through slipping serves, and the way to survive it is patience, serve protection, and high-percentage play - not chasing the run.
